summary_md: The perception service is the PC's one pair of eyes on the game: an always-on standalone process, not elevated, that the babysitter or any gamelab command that needs it starts automatically (detached, through Windows' WMI service), never the elevated player. Its main thread is the frame loop, 15 frames a second; around it run a dozen helper threads (a pipe listener, a reader and a writer per attached command, a watchdog, the telemetry, console and GC writers, the rolling recording's three threads, the Lie Detector watchers) and a few worker-thread pools for the picture matching. It starts short-lived child processes itself, never you: the mini-game tracker while a Lie Detector alarm is up, a part writer for each save of the rolling recording, and, rarely, the C compiler when its C library isn't built yet.

processes.plain_md:
**What it is.** The one process that looks at the game for everybody. It is its own Windows process (`python -m gamelab perceive`, usually `--map 10002073`), not elevated, at normal priority, and without a window when it is started automatically. Only one runs on the PC: it holds a named Windows lock (the mutex `Local\gamelab-perceive`), and a second copy prints that one is running and exits at once. (`perceive --frames DIR`, an offline copy that plays saved pictures, has its own lock and pipe and can run beside it.)

**Who starts it, and when.** Normally nobody types it. Two things start it automatically, whichever comes first:
- the babysitter (a PowerShell loop outside the repo, below) starts one within 5 s whenever no `gamelab perceive` is in the process list: `--map 10002073`, its console appended to `D:/MapleHelper-scratch/live/perceive.log`;
- any gamelab command that needs to see the game (hunt, tour, nav, probe, pet (the babysitter's `pet --every` too), `nav --park`, map, watch, `hunt look`, `window --recover`, `keys --read`, `stats --read`) starts one itself when it can't reach one and no service holds the lock (`service.ensure`, at most every 10 s, on the command's own map, its console appended to `gamelab/lab/perceive.log`). So a hunt that Claude runs brings the service up by itself. The command waits up to 20 s for it; the first state comes about 2 s after the start.

Both ask Windows' WMI service to create a hidden `cmd.exe` that runs Python (a command does it through a short `powershell.exe`), so the service is not its starter's child: it keeps running after the command or the babysitter ends, and it gets none of their environment variables (hence the settings on the command line). The elevated player never starts it. You can also run it by hand in a terminal and stop it with Ctrl+C.

**How long it lives.** It is meant to run all the time; with no game window it just waits and says why. It ends on Ctrl+C or `--minutes` (then it closes cleanly: lets the commands go, stops the tracker child, and writes the saves still queued, an alarm's clip cut short, 2 minutes at most), when someone kills it (Task Manager, Stop-Process: no gamelab command does), or when its watchdog ends it with exit code 3 because the frame loop hung for 10 s. It never restarts itself: the babysitter's next loop or a command's next `ensure` starts a fresh one, and the 5 minutes of rolling recording it held in memory are lost.

**What it does with the game.** 15 times a second it copies the game window off the screen (Windows' desktop duplication, DXGI; it never brings the game forward), works out her place, HP, MP and EXP, every monster with its track, and the drops, and hands each result to every attached command through the named pipe `\\.\pipe\gamelab-perceive` (the pictures through shared memory). It also writes telemetry for the mini-map, keeps the last 5 minutes as a rolling recording, and during a Lie Detector alarm follows the two mini-games. It never presses a key: its few mouse moves and clicks during an alarm are plans it hands to the elevated player.

**The babysitter, as found.** A PowerShell script outside the repo, `D:/MapleHelper-scratch/live/babysit3.ps1` (the README's path under `pconst/finish/` no longer exists): an endless loop every 5 s that also starts and stops the pet feeder around hunts and hands the recording over from the old recorder. Nothing starts the babysitter automatically: no task in Windows' Task Scheduler, nothing in D:/MapleHelper-scratch or C:/Users/Admin/.claude. Its header says to start it once, detached through WMI "so it outlives Claude Code", by you or a Claude session. At this check (2026-11-16) neither the babysitter nor a service was running, the babysitter's logs were not on disk, and the last service start on record (`gamelab/lab/perceive.log`, 2026-11-07 06:37) came from a command's `ensure`, the only thing that writes that log.
processes.expected_start: automatically, whichever comes first: the babysitter (within 5 s whenever none runs, while the babysitter itself runs) or the first gamelab command that needs to see the game and can't reach one (service.ensure, at most every 10 s; this includes the hunts Claude runs); or you, by hand in a terminal; never the elevated player

components.name: The frame loop
components.started_by: `cmd_perceive` calls `Service.serve` right after start-up; it is the process's main thread
components.does: Every 1/15 s: takes the next frame from the screen capture, runs one pass of the world step on it, and hands the result out: the picture into the shared-memory ring, the state to every client's writer queue, the frame to the rolling recording and the Lie Detector watchers, the state to the telemetry publisher. A frame the game drew nothing new on, that nobody asked about, is skipped. Between frames it waits on the inbox the reader threads fill and merges what the commands ask for (drops to search on the next frame, a full-size frame). It builds a new 'run' (that map's templates, new rings, every client told) when the game is first seen and whenever an attached command needs another map: a hunting command always gets its map, any other command only while no hunting command holds the current one. With no game window it sends a 'not visible' state every 0.25 s. Every 10 s it prints a status line (frames a second, who is attached). With `--frames DIR` it plays saved PNGs instead, offline, with no telemetry, recording or Lie Detector watchers.
components.rate: 15 frames a second (localization.rate.HZ); a pass takes about 10-60 ms

talks_to.what: the next frame of the game, or why there is none
one frame in, a WorldState (plain, picklable data) out

talks_to.via: the deque Service._inbox under the threading.Condition Service._cond
talks_to.what: asks, throws and full-frame asks in; the loop waits on the Condition until the next frame is due
the state, pickled once for all clients; welcomes and new-run notices
the look frame (and full-size frames for 'full' asks)
the frame, 15 a second at most
the newest frame, only while the alarm is up
frames while the alarm is up and 90 s after
each state, for telemetry
'I went round' at every turn

components.name: The screen capture
components.runs_as: library code on the caller's thread
components.started_by: made with each run by `screen_world` (ScreenFrames on the process's one grabber, `capture.shared`)
components.lives: as long as the process (the grabber); the ScreenFrames as long as its run
components.does: Runs on the frame loop's thread. Finds the game window, checks it can be read (wholly on screen, in front, not covered, 1366x768 or 1920x1080, not moved during the shot, not a stale picture), and copies its client area from DXGI desktop duplication; if DXGI fails it uses mss for 10 s and tries again. It never brings the game forward. With the recording on it also asks which other windows are over the game before and after each shot. A frame that fails its checks makes the eyes recover (the duplication made afresh).
components.rate: once a frame, 15 a second

talks_to.via: DXGI desktop duplication (mss as fallback); the window's place and state from Windows
talks_to.what: the game's pixels, read only
a Frame: the picture, its time, whether it shows the game and why not

components.name: The world step (one pass a frame)
components.runs_as: library code on the caller's thread
components.started_by: made for each run by `screen_world` (Eyes, Senses, WorldStep for that map)
components.lives: one run: replaced (and closed) when the map changes

Turns one frame into a WorldState: her look (her place by her name tag, the mini-map dot and the scene, HP, MP, EXP), the whole screen's search for monsters, each monster matched to its track (id, place, HP bar, death), her touches, and the drops asked for plus a strip of drops in view by rotation. The state is plain data, so it can be pickled down the pipe.

components.lives: the 'wide' pool and the monster search's and the drops' pools belong to a run (a new run makes new ones, the old ones end with it); the name tag's, the scene's and her poses' pools are made once and kept for the process

See the process `native-build`.

The frame loop writes each frame into the next slot; a command copies the one its state names, by number, in its own process (a slot already overwritten comes back as lost). The welcome message tells each command the rings' names.

components.started_by: `Service.listen`, at start-up, before the frame loop's first frame
components.does: Opens the named pipe `\\.\pipe\gamelab-perceive` (Python's multiprocessing.connection, with a random key written with the service's pid to `gamelab/lab/perceive.json`, where commands find it) and accepts each command that connects, giving it a reader thread and a writer thread. Thread name `perceive-accept`.

components.started_by: the pipe listener, when a command connects
components.lives: until that command says `bye` or its pipe closes (then the client is dropped)
components.does: Reads what the command sends. `hello` (its name, pid, whether it sends keys or hunts, its map) is answered here: with a welcome naming the run's rings, or with a refusal when it hunts on another map while another hunting command holds the current one. A command on another map that isn't refused has the frame loop build a run for its map (a viewer's or the pet's only while no hunting command holds the map). `status` is answered here. `ask` (what to search on the next frame), `throw` (she attacked) and `full` (send a full-size frame) go into the frame loop's inbox. When the command leaves and no hunting command is left, the service moves to the map of the newest command that sends keys. Thread name `perceive-reader-<id>`.

components.name: One writer per attached command
components.started_by: the client's Writer, made when the command connects
components.lives: until the command is dropped or the pipe breaks
components.does: Sends each frame's state (a few KB, pickled once by the frame loop) down that command's pipe. It holds at most the newest 64 states (about 4 s); older ones are dropped and a `gap` message says how many, so a command that stops reading never holds up the frame loop. Welcomes, new-run notices and full-frame answers are never dropped and go first. Thread name `perceive-writer-<id>`.

components.name: The watchdog
components.started_by: `Service.serve` at start-up
components.does: Once a second it checks when the frame loop last went round. If it hasn't for 10 s (60 s while a new run's templates load), it logs why, flushes the console and telemetry and ends the whole process with exit code 3 (`os._exit`), so that the babysitter or a command's `ensure` starts a fresh service; the pipe and the mutex go with the process. A hang that holds Python's lock stops this thread too. Thread name `perceive-watchdog`.

components.runs_as: library code on the caller's thread
components.started_by: `cmd_perceive` makes it; the frame loop calls it with each state

It only queues them: writing is the telemetry writer's job.

processes.plain_md:
**What it is.** A short-lived helper process of the perception service that follows the Lie Detector mouse mini-game's target: `python -m gamelab.control.lie_tracking <gamelab/lab/lie_target> 15`, its own Windows process, hidden (no window), below-normal priority, not elevated.

**Who starts it, and when.** Never you or the babysitter. The service's mini-game watcher thread starts it as soon as it sees the alarm file `gamelab/lab/ALARM.json` (written by the elevated player's watchdog when it sees a Lie Detector, or by a command that sees one), and stops it 60 s after the alarm has gone (a `quit` message, then a kill if it doesn't end within 5 s). It also ends when the service closes (a `quit`) or dies (its stdin closes). So it exists only for a minute or two per Lie Detector.

**Why apart.** Following the target takes about 52-64 ms a frame with OpenCV on 6 to 12 threads (it uses 6); inside the service, where OpenCV has one thread and the frame loop shares Python's lock, it took 78 ms, more than the 66 ms between frames at 15 a second.

**What it does.** It never looks at the screen or touches the game: board pictures come down its stdin, one each time it says it is ready; it writes each round's answers to `gamelab/lab/lie_target/<time>.jsonl` and sends the target's position back up its stdout. The service then moves the mouse through the elevated player. Its stderr goes nowhere, so its failures show only as `error` replies in the service's log.
processes.expected_start: spawned by perceive (its mini-game watcher thread) when the Lie Detector alarm goes up

components.name: The tracker loop
components.started_by: the process's start (`serve`, from its `__main__`)
components.does: Says `ready`, then reads messages one by one: `begin` opens the round's file and makes a fresh target tracker; each `frame` (the board's 750x500 picture) is one step of the tracker, an answer line written and `ready` sent back with it; `end` writes the round's summary line (frames, answers, skipped, median and worst ms) and replies `ended`. An error is replied as `error` and the next message taken.
components.rate: one frame at a time, as sent (about 52-64 ms each)

talks_to.via: stdin (pickled begin, frame, end, quit) / stdout (pickled ready, ended, error)
talks_to.what: board pictures in, the target's position out
the frame's work spread over threads

components.name: The tracker's worker threads
components.started_by: the tracker, at its first frame (`lie_target._pool`); OpenCV's own threads at start-up

processes.plain_md:
**What it is.** A one-shot helper process of the perception service that writes one saved stretch of the rolling recording to disk: `python -m gamelab.control.partwriter`, its own Windows process, hidden, below-normal priority (Idle if the service runs at Idle), its threads at the lowest priority, not elevated.

**Who starts it, and when.** Never you or the babysitter. The service's saver thread starts one per save, one at a time: after a Lie Detector cycle (the 5 minutes before it, then its clip), for a Truth Booth with no test seen, and for each `python -m gamelab save-recent`. It ends as soon as its part is written; the service kills it after 600 s and then writes the part itself, as it does when the child can't start or fails.

**Why apart.** Encoding is heavy: a 120 s save written inside the service made the frame loop drop to 8-10 frames a second (Python's lock); written apart, the loop barely notices.

**What it does.** The service pipes the compressed frames down its stdin; it reads them all, decodes them and encodes them to JPEG (PNG for an alarm's clip, a Truth Booth save and a `save-recent` asked lossless) on 4 threads (2 while a hunting command is attached), writes the folder (the frames, `index.jsonl`, `summary.json`) and prints one JSON line with the summary. It never looks at the screen or touches the game. If the service dies while still sending, it gets a broken stdin, says `error` and exits.
processes.expected_start: spawned by perceive (its recording's saver thread), one per save

components.name: The part writer's main thread
components.started_by: the process's start (`partwriter.main`)
components.lives: until the part is written (or it fails)
components.does: Reads a header (the folder, the save's info, fps, png or not, how many threads, how many moments) and then every moment from stdin into memory, writes the part with `rolling.write_part`, and prints `{"summary": ...}` (exit 0) or `{"error": ...}` (exit 1).
components.rate: once

talks_to.via: stdin (pickled header and moments) / stdout (one JSON line)
talks_to.what: the frames in, the summary out
chains of frames to encode

components.name: The encoder threads
components.started_by: `rolling.write_part`, inside the main thread's call
components.does: Decodes each chain of frames (a whole frame and its differences) and encodes them to JPEG or PNG, a batch at a time, at the lowest thread priority. 4 threads, or 2 while a hunting command is attached to the service. Pool name `rolling-writer`.
components.rate: all the part's frames, as fast as the CPU allows (300 s of frames took 24-31 s in the service)

talks_to.what: encoded frames, written to the folder by the main thread
